Their mother lifted the key from her neck. “Stay together,” she said, and led them to the cellar door.

Mara had passed it every day of her life. It was a narrow thing, painted the same white as the wall, with no handle on the outside. Now a line of gold shone beneath it.

The girl touched the wood. “It knows we’re here.”

Their mother fitted the key into a keyhole Mara had never noticed. It turned by itself.

Cold air breathed up the stairs, carrying the smell of wet leaves and woodsmoke. Somewhere below, a bell rang once.

Elsie gripped Mara’s sleeve. “What’s down there?”

“The garden,” their mother said.

“That’s impossible,” Mara replied.

“So was the seed.”

The door swung inward. Beyond it stretched a path beneath a midnight sky, though it was still morning above them. Ash trees crowded the way, their bare branches reaching over a stream of bright, running water.

At the far end stood a woman in a green coat.

The girl hurried down two steps, then stopped. “Grandmother?”

The woman raised her face. She looked just as she did in the faded photograph on the mantel—young, smiling, and not a day older.

Their mother gripped the key until her knuckles whitened. “You said you’d never come back.”

“I didn’t,” the woman answered. “I sent for them.”

Behind her, the trees shivered. From somewhere among their branches came three soft knocks.
